title: Savitri's three-night vow
hookLine: Savitri knows her husband's death day, tells no one, and keeps a vow of fasting for three nights
carry: a vrata: a fast held as prayer for someone
last: THE GAYATRI ASKS THE LIGHT TO WAKE OUR MINDS.

lines: NO ONE IN THE HERMITAGE HEARD.
cards: The warning was spoken once, in a palace. When the sage Narada said that Satyavan would die within the year, he said it at a royal court, to Savitri and her father.
Then the wedding happened in a forest hermitage, far from that court. Satyavan didn't hear the warning. His parents didn't.
The hermits didn't. So Savitri moves into her new home carrying a sentence about her husband that nobody around her has heard. Today: what she does with it, and what she doesn't say.

teach.b: First, what she does. She takes off her jewels and wears the rough cloth of the forest. She looks after her husband's parents, an old king who has lost his sight and his kingdom, and his wife.
And through all of it, the epic says, Narada's words stay in her mind, day and night. She is counting. She doesn't tell Satyavan or his parents.
The epic never says why; some readers hear mercy, sparing them a year of dread, some hear resolve.
When the day draws near, she does the one thing she can: she takes a vow, a vrata, fasting and standing through three nights. Her father-in-law worries it's too hard.
She tells him gently that she will finish it, because it was undertaken with resolve. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: A VRATA: A VOW, A FAST, A RESOLVE
teach.b: A vrata is one of the most common Hindu practices there is: a vow, begun with a stated resolve, a sankalpa, kept with fasting or restraint, and finished, offered for something you care about. Often for someone else.
Savitri's is the most well-known; many married women still keep a fast in her name. Mothers and grandmothers fast for a child's health or a grandchild's exam.

It isn't a bargain with God, many teachers say; it's prayer you hold in your body, so the person you're praying for is with you all day. And look at Savitri's silence again. She isn't hiding from the truth.
She's turning her fear into a vow, eyes open, counting toward the day, getting ready with her own body.

how: Hindus keep vratas, vows begun with a stated resolve and kept with fasting or restraint, for themselves and often for others: some married women keep a fast in Savitri's name, and parents and grandparents keep weekday or festival fasts for a family member's health or success.

o: a wife who told the whole hermitage her fears
a wife who turned a hard secret into a vow of fasting
a bride who forgot a warning until it came true

p: spoke the warning at her father's court
a vow kept with fasting or restraint
the resolve stated at the start
worried her vow was too hard

s: Savitri told Satyavan what Narada had said
she told no one; the warning stayed with her, day and night.
a vrata is often kept as prayer for someone else
Savitri's three-night fast was for her husband; Hindu parents and grandparents still fast for family.
in Hindu practice a vow is a bargain: fast, and God must pay out
many teachers describe it as prayer held in the body, offered, not a deal.

games.q: you're Savitri. you know what Narada said, and the day is close. your husband and his parents know nothing. what do you do?
o: take a vrata: fast and keep vigil three nights, and finish it.
ask your father to bring him back to the palace.
games.why: she takes the vow and finishes it, and on the last morning she asks to walk into the forest beside him.

practice: Bring to mind one person you're worried for right now. Make a small resolve for them, a sankalpa, something you can keep today: skip one treat, keep one hour quiet, say one prayer at a set time.
Say it inwardly, plainly: today, for them, I'll do this. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, let it simply be a way of keeping them with you all day.

wordCard.voice: Savitri. The young wife who heard a hard truth at her father's court, carried it alone into the forest, and turned it into a vow. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, vrata: a vow, kept with fasting or restraint; Savitri's was three nights.

carryVoice: Your line: a vrata, a fast held as prayer for someone. Savitri kept hers for three nights. Go gently, and come back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Savitri in the hermitage; Narada's words in her mind; the three-night vow; Dyumatsena's worry; she asks to go to the forest with Satyavan)
